strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem — mitigating sensitive-attribute bias in medical image diagnosis — and the causal framing (allowing the effect of S on the prediction only when it is mediated by the true diagnosis Y) is conceptually sensible for clinical settings.

The proposed pipeline is reasonable and non-trivial: an MI-based pretraining stage for representation/data utility combined with adversarial mask generation using a Y-conditioned discriminator; learning an input perturbation that removes S-dependent features while retaining diagnostic ones is an appealing extension of adversarial debiasing to medical images.

The empirical results are consistent across three datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, TCGA-LUAD) and three fairness metrics (DP, EO, ADF), with roughly retained accuracy (Table 1), and the ablations over backbones (ResNet18/50, ViT; Table 2) and hyperparameters eta/alpha/beta (Tables 3-5) provide some insight into the fairness-accuracy trade-off.

The Grad-CAM analysis (Fig. 4) offers qualitative support for the claim that the method decouples the image regions driving the prediction and the sensitive-attribute classifier, relative to the vanilla model.
Reproducibility-relevant details are provided (public datasets, hyperparameter values, hardware and software environment in Appendix A, code promised).
weaknesses: The theoretical contribution is overstated and partly incorrect. (a) DE(S)=0 is essentially the already-known 'no direct discrimination' criterion in the causal fairness literature (e.g., Zhang et al. 2016 [36], which is cited), so the claim that 'previous fairness metrics are agnostic to causal modeling' is not tenable. (b) The sufficiency direction of Theorem 2 is an immediate consequence of the data-processing inequality, because the prediction is a function of X (the 'complete mediator' assumption is unnecessary), and the necessity 'proof' provides no counterexample and is not a proof. (c) The text inverts its own theorem: the statement on p.5 that 'Theorem 2 concludes that I(S;Yhat|Y)=0 is a sufficient condition for I(S;X|Y)=0' contradicts Theorem 2 and is exactly the direction needed to justify ADF as a metric. As proven, ADF=0 is only necessary for DF, so the justification for the proposed metric does not hold.

Nonstandard causal terminology and an inconsistent SCM: Fig. 1 contains no S->Yhat edge, yet the criterion is described as removing the 'direct effect'; the path pi_d={S->X->Yhat} is called the 'direct path' and pi_i={S->Y->X->Yhat} the 'indirect path', which conflicts with the standard definitions of direct/indirect effects used by the cited causal-inference references (e.g., Pearl [27], Zhang et al. [36]).

Theory-method gap: the analysis concerns I(S;X|Y)=0 / DE(S)=0 on the clean input X, while the algorithm minimizes I(Shat;S) on perturbed inputs X~ = X (+) g(X) with a frozen feature extractor. Eq. 8 is asserted rather than derived, and no argument links the adversarial objective (Eqs. 8-12) or the entropy term alpha*H(Shat) to the stated criterion, so the 'theoretically grounded' claim is not supported.

Key method details are missing: the architectures/parameterization of the mask generator g and the discriminator d_Y, how the noise strength eta is applied (it appears only in the ablations), what 'iteratively adding with both upper and lower constraints' in Eq. 4 means, and how the MI estimator is jointly optimized with theta.

The experimental evidence is not rigorous enough for the strength of the claims: no multiple seeds, error bars, or significance tests, despite accuracy differences as small as 85.80 vs 85.87 on CheXpert; only two adversarial baselines (AD, FAAP) are compared, with no comparison to causal-fairness baselines (e.g., [36]) or to TARA [25], which the introduction itself identifies as a leading algorithmic approach; simple reweighting/group-DRO baselines are also absent.

Only a single sensitive attribute (gender) is evaluated on all three datasets, even though race is the motivating example; there is no subgroup analysis and no discussion of whether legitimate sex-related diagnostic signal (which the criterion explicitly allows to pass through Y) is preserved.

The 'data utility' claims are overstated: the reported AUCs of roughly 60-75% (Fig. 3) are far below standard MIMIC-CXR benchmarks, yet are described as demonstrating robustness, and the contribution of the MI-based pretraining is never isolated by an ablation.
The explanation analysis is purely qualitative (Fig. 4); no quantitative localization or faithfulness measure is provided to support the disentanglement claim.

Presentation and reproducibility concerns: 'SCM of rural model' in the Fig. 1 caption, several reference typos, unclear notation, no explicit limitations discussion, and an abstract claim of 'preserving diagnostic accuracy' that is stronger than the results (accuracy is consistently slightly below the vanilla baseline on all three datasets).

ADF conditions on Y, which is assumed to be the true diagnosis, but the MIMIC-CXR/CheXpert labels are NLP-extracted proxies with substantial noise; the consequences for both the criterion and the metric are not discussed.

strengths: Proposes a principled causal fairness criterion, Diagnosis Fairness (DF), that distinguishes the direct effect of a sensitive attribute (S→X→Ŷ) from its indirect, clinically legitimate effect (S→Y→X→Ŷ), which is a meaningful conceptual advance over bias-agnostic fairness metrics used in medical imaging.

Introduces the Approximate Diagnosis Fairness (ADF) metric I(S;Ŷ|Y) as a practical surrogate, and provides theoretical analysis (Theorems 1 and 2) attempting to bridge the adversarial training objective with the fairness criterion.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three real-world medical datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, TCGA-LUAD), comparing against Vanilla, AD, and FAAP baselines, with consistent reductions in EO, DP, and ADF while keeping accuracy comparable.

Includes a broad set of supporting studies: architecture ablation (ResNet18/50, ViT), hyperparameter ablations on η, α, β, a data-utility assessment over eight downstream tasks, and a GradCAM explainability analysis showing reduced overlap between the diagnosis and sensitive-attribute heatmaps.
Good reproducibility practices: hyperparameter settings, dataset splits, software/hardware environment, and a stated commitment to release code, conda environment, and Docker container.
weaknesses: Theorem 2 is internally inconsistent: its statement claims I(S;X|Y)=0 is a 'sufficient and necessary' condition for I(S;Ŷ|Y)=0, yet the necessity proof explicitly constructs a case showing it is NOT necessary. This contradiction undermines the theoretical justification of ADF as an evaluation metric and should be corrected.

The theoretical analysis assumes X is a 'complete mediator' between Ŷ and (Y,S). This is a strong assumption that is unlikely to hold for high-dimensional medical images, and it is not discussed as a limitation, weakening the claimed soundness of the causal framework.

The sensitive attribute is restricted to gender in all experiments, despite the paper motivating race and other demographic attributes. Claims about generalizing to race are therefore unsupported by the evidence presented.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported. Given the very small accuracy gaps and the medical-AI context, the reliability of the reported differences (especially the near-zero EO/DP values for the proposed method) cannot be assessed.

The proposed method is consistently slightly less accurate than the Vanilla baseline on all three datasets (e.g., MIMIC 84.26 vs 85.46, TCGA 97.85 vs 98.47), which only partially supports the 'without sacrificing diagnostic accuracy' claim.

The connection between the practical adversarial objective (minimizing I(Ŝ;S)) and the theoretical condition I(S;X|Y)=0 is heuristic rather than rigorously established; the discriminator predicts S from masked input conditioned on Y, but it is not formally shown that this drives I(S;X|Y) to zero.

It is unclear how the generator-produced masks behave at inference time and whether applying them to test inputs preserves clinical validity; the pipeline's deployment story (masking test images before feeding the frozen model) is not clearly discussed.
The novelty relative to existing causal-fairness (Pearl, Zhang et al.) and adversarial-debiasing (AD, FAAP) work is moderate; the main novel elements are the application domain and the ADF metric.

strengths: Proposes a coherent and well-motivated causal framing for fairness in medical imaging that distinguishes direct (S→X→Ŷ) and indirect (S→Y→X→Ŷ) effects of sensitive attributes, and introduces a new criterion (Diagnosis Fairness, DF) and a practical metric (Approximate Diagnosis Fairness, ADF = I(S;Ŷ|Y)) that are conceptually clean and easy to interpret.

Empirical improvements in fairness metrics are substantial and consistent across three datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, TCGA-LUAD): ADF is reduced by ~5-9x, and traditional metrics like EO and DP are also markedly reduced while accuracy remains close to vanilla, indicating the gains generalize beyond the authors' own metric.

Includes a thoughtful explainability analysis (GradCAM) showing that the vanilla model's prediction heatmaps overlap with sensitive-attribute heatmaps, whereas the proposed method separates them—this qualitatively supports the disentanglement claim.
Ablation studies over the noise strength η, entropy regularization α, loss regularization β, and different backbones (ResNet18/50, ViT) give reasonable insight into the trade-offs of the method.
Provides code/environment details (PyTorch, Docker, conda) and commits to releasing implementations, which helps reproducibility.

The paper correctly identifies the insufficiency of naive TCE=0 fairness in the medical context, where the sensitive attribute may legitimately correlate with true pathology, and argues for pruning only the direct effect.
weaknesses: All experiments use only gender as the sensitive attribute, despite the abstract and introduction emphasizing race. Race-related bias is arguably more consequential in clinical AI and would provide a much stronger and more distinctive evaluation. This mismatch between claimed scope and actual experiments weakens the contribution.

The theoretical results are not as airtight as claimed. In the proof of Theorem 1 (Eq. 17), the last line reads DE(S) = C·Σ_Y(P(Y|S⁻_{πi}) − P(Y|S⁻_{πi})) = 0, which is trivially zero because both terms are identical—there appears to be a typo that undermines confidence in the derivation. Theorem 2 additionally relies on an unstated 'complete mediator' assumption about X that is not justified for the proposed masking-based intervention.

The ADF evaluation metric I(S;Ŷ|Y) is central to the paper's claims, yet the paper does not clearly describe how mutual information is estimated at evaluation time (which estimator, which batch size, nats vs bits, and stability across runs). Without this, the reported ADF values are hard to interpret or reproduce.

Experimental setup is under-specified for a top-tier venue: no confidence intervals or multiple seeds, a 90/10 train/test split without clarifying whether it is patient-level (important for MIMIC/CheXpert where multiple images share patients), and no statistical significance testing on the observed fairness improvements.

Baselines are limited to Vanilla, AD, and FAAP. Notably, Madras et al. (2018) 'Learning Adversarially Fair and Transferable Representations' is cited ([21]) and is very close in spirit (adversarial debiasing with an information-theoretic objective) but is not compared against; this makes the claimed novelty harder to assess.

Accuracy slightly decreases in every reported setting (e.g., MIMIC 85.46→84.26, TCGA 98.47→97.85). While the drops are small, the paper does not discuss whether such degradations are clinically acceptable, nor does it analyze the fairness-accuracy Pareto frontier rigorously.

The assumed SCM (S→Y→X→Ŷ) is debatable: treating the sensitive attribute as a cause of the true diagnosis Y is unusual for demographic attributes, and the paper does not carefully defend this edge direction or consider alternatives (e.g., S as a confounder of X and Y).

The masking generator's ability to suppress sensitive-attribute information while preserving pathology-relevant features is asserted rather than analyzed. There is no quantitative study of how much diagnostic signal is lost, nor of failure cases where the mask removes clinically relevant content (e.g., breast tissue in female chest X-rays, which the paper itself acknowledges).

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated problem: Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness (PSCF) is causal-principled but has been limited to low-dimensional/tabular settings, and the paper proposes a tractable reduction that is plausibly deployable on high-dimensional medical images.

The core theoretical reformulation is clean and useful: reducing PSCF to the conditional independence constraint I(S; X | Y) = 0 (Theorem 1) and bridging it to Equalized Odds (Theorem 2) gives a discriminative objective in place of intractable counterfactual density estimation. The authors are commendably explicit that the condition is sufficient but not necessary (Appendix A remark).

The synthetic-SCM experiment (Table 8) is a strong piece of evidence: it directly measures ground-truth |DE(S)| and |IE(S)|, showing SPARC drives |DE(S)| from 0.284 to 0.027 while preserving |IE(S)| at 0.171 (vs. AD, which collapses |IE(S)| to 0.061). This is exactly the kind of validation needed for a path-specific claim, and it is rare to see it done.

Experimental coverage is broad and well controlled: three datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, TCGA-LUAD), three backbones (ResNet18/50, ViT), two sensitive attributes (gender, age), ablations over noise strength η and loss weights α, β, a validation-vs-test hyperparameter generalization check (Table 9), and a computational-cost breakdown (Table 7, +12% FLOPs).

Fairness gains over adversarial baselines are substantial and consistent (e.g., EOd on CheXpert 1.20×10⁻² vs. 3.07×10⁻² for Group-DRO; MIMIC-CXR EOd 2.25 vs. 7.38 for AD) with only modest accuracy cost, and the GradCAM overlap analysis between Ŷ- and Ŝ-heatmaps is a sensible qualitative corroboration of the disentanglement claim.
Reproducibility is taken seriously: fixed hyperparameters, 5 seeds with std. devs, hardware/software environment, Docker/Conda details, and a promise of released code and environments.
weaknesses: Novelty relative to existing adversarial fairness methods is thinner than the framing suggests. The instantiated method is a conditional adversarial-masking scheme with an MI-preservation term (Eqs. 8–14), which is conceptually close to Adversarial Debiasing [52] and especially to FAAP [48] — the latter is even listed as a baseline. The paper does not isolate what the causal/path-specific formulation contributes beyond “condition the discriminator on Y.” A controlled ablation (e.g., an unconditional vs. Y-conditional discriminator, or a masked-input variant of FAAP) is needed to substantiate the central novelty claim.

Theory–practice gap is under-acknowledged. Theorems 1–2 are population-level statements under a specific SCM in which X is a complete mediator between Ŷ and (Y, S) (no direct S → Ŷ edge) and interventional ignorability/consistency hold. The deployed algorithm (a finite-capacity generator/discriminator saddle-point plus a JSD MI surrogate) only approximates I(S; X̃ | Y) = 0 on the perturbed input, and there is no analysis of estimation error, discriminator capacity, or equilibrium existence. The only empirical check of the gap is a 1-D synthetic SCM, which does not test the high-dimensional regime that motivates the paper.

The “preserve the indirect path” claim is weakly supported. Maximizing I(X̃; E) (Eq. 10) preserves generic task-relevant information, not specifically the S → Y → X pathway; the indirect-effect preservation in practice rests mostly on the β·I(Ŷ; Y) term and the observed accuracy retention. There is no direct measurement of IE preservation in the image datasets (only in the toy SCM), so the paper's central “remove the direct path, keep the indirect path” promise is only partially verified where it matters.

No causal-fairness baseline is evaluated in the high-dimensional setting. The authors dismiss Chiappa [9]/Chikahara [10] as “fundamentally inapplicable,” but a reduced-feature version (e.g., running them on frozen pretrained embeddings) would be a fair and informative comparison, and would strengthen the “scalability” claim far more than comparisons to non-causal baselines alone.

Key methodological details are underspecified. The mask operator X ⊕ g(X) is described as “iterative addition with both upper and lower constraints” without a formal definition or pseudocode; η’s relationship to the mask is only explained post hoc in the ablation. Similarly, the EOd estimator (Eq. 16 / Eq. 23) is given as an information-theoretic quantity with citations but no concrete estimator or its bias/variance behavior, even though EOd is the headline fairness number in every table. The training schedule for alternating generator/discriminator updates is not given.

Some of the framing is conceptually contestable. Treating all S-correlated information in the image as “unfair direct effect” (e.g., the breast-region example in §4.5) risks discarding legitimate anatomy/body-habitus signals that are diagnostically informative; the accuracy drops on MIMIC-CXR (85.46 → 84.26) and TCGA-LUAD (98.47 → 97.85) relative to Vanilla may partly reflect this, and the paper does not examine whether the removed information is medically relevant. A discussion of this trade-off and its clinical implications would improve the contribution.

Minor presentation issues: the code URL is left blank (“The code is available at .”), the Baselines/Datasets/Metrics text is duplicated verbatim between §4.1–4.2 and Appendix B, and the main table omits any variance-aware significance statement for the SPARC-vs-baseline gaps even though std. devs are reported.

strengths: The core insight—reducing Path-Specific Counterfactual Fairness to the causal conditional independence constraint I(S; X | Y) = 0—is elegant and well-motivated. It replaces intractable marginal potential-outcome estimation with a discriminative objective that is genuinely tractable in high-dimensional modalities, directly addressing the stated failure mode of prior PSCF work on tabular data.

The theoretical development is sound and clearly presented. Theorem 1 (Derivability) provides a sufficiency proof that is worked through carefully in Appendix A, and Theorem 2 (Observability) connects the training objective to Equalized Odds, giving practitioners a measurable fairness signal to monitor. The Remark on sufficiency vs. necessity is intellectually honest about the stricter nature of the constraint.

The experimental evidence is reasonably comprehensive for the claims: three datasets (MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, TCGA-LUAD), five baselines, ablations over backbone architecture, sensitive attribute, and all three hyperparameters (η, α, β), plus explainability analysis with GradCAM showing disentanglement of Ŷ- and Ŝ-relevant regions.

The synthetic-SCM validation (Table 8) is a particularly valuable addition, since it directly verifies that SPARC reduces the ground-truth |DE(S)| while preserving |IE(S)|, rather than only relying on observational fairness metrics. The contrast with AD (which collapses IE) supports the path-specific claim.

Reproducibility is well handled: code link, hyperparameter settings, environment specification (Conda/Docker), compute cost analysis (Table 7), and validation-vs-test hyperparameter transfer (Table 9). The reported improvements are unlikely to be artifacts of tuning.
The paper is clearly written, well-structured, and the framework figure (Fig. 2) and SCM diagram (Fig. 1) communicate the pipeline and causal assumptions effectively.
weaknesses: The central theoretical result is a sufficiency condition, and the authors themselves acknowledge (Remark, p. 21) that I(S; X | Y) = 0 is stricter than PSCF: it suppresses all residual X–S dependence given Y, including directions that contribute negligibly to Ŷ. While the synthetic experiment suggests this gap is small in practice (|DE| = 0.027 vs. target 0), the practical cost of over-constraining on real high-dimensional data is not quantified beyond this single synthetic setting.

The notation around X is ambiguous. In the SCM (Fig. 1, Definitions 2–3) X is a mediator between S and Ŷ, but in Eq. 8 the model operates on X̃ = X ⊕ g(X) as an input-modality representation. The relationship between the mediator X in the causal graph and the network's internal representation is not made precise, which makes it harder to assess exactly what the constraint I(S; X | Y) = 0 is enforced on in practice.

The empirical gains, while consistent, are sometimes modest. On TCGA-LUAD, SPARC's accuracy (97.85) is actually below Vanilla (98.47) and its EOd improvement over Group-DRO is incremental. The abstract's claim of outperforming baselines would benefit from a clearer discussion of when the trade-off is favorable versus not.

The adversarial min–max optimization with an MI estimator is notoriously unstable, yet the paper provides no discussion of training stability, convergence behavior, or sensitivity to the generator/discriminator update schedule. This matters for reproducibility of the reported trade-offs.

The claim of scalability is only demonstrated on medical imaging at moderate scale; no experiments on larger-scale or more heterogeneous modalities (e.g., natural images or multimodal clinical data) are presented to substantiate the broad 'scalable' framing, and no comparison against other adaptable causal-fairness baselines beyond AD is included.

It is not fully clarified whether the conditional discriminator d_Y(X̃, Y) uses ground-truth labels at training time only (as seems intended) and whether any label leakage affects the reported fairness metrics at test time; the fairness metrics condition on Y, so the evaluation protocol should be explicit on this point.

The explainability analysis is qualitative (heatmap overlap); no quantitative disentanglement metric is reported, so the claim of 'clear separation' between Ŷ and Ŝ regions rests on visual inspection.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and well-motivated limitation: exact PSCF relies on estimating marginal potential outcome probabilities, which is intractable in high-dimensional modalities like medical images. Recasting this as a trainable discriminative objective is a worthwhile direction.

Provides theory (Theorem 1 on derivability and Theorem 2 on observability) that connects the training objective to PSCF and to a standard, measurable fairness criterion (Equalized Odds), giving the method an interpretable grounding.

The synthetic-SCM validation (Table 8) is the most convincing evidence: SPARC reduces the direct effect |DE(S)| from 0.284 to 0.027 while preserving the indirect effect |IE(S)| near the ground truth (0.171 vs 0.182), whereas AD collapses the indirect effect (0.061). This directly supports the path-specific claim.

Experiments are reasonably thorough: three datasets, three backbones, ablations on noise strength, entropy weight α, loss weight β, an age-based sensitive-attribute ablation, hyperparameter generalization (Table 9), computational-cost analysis, and reproducibility details (environment, Docker, hyperparameters).
Consistent fairness improvements over AD, FAAP, SUBG, and Group-DRO across datasets, with accuracy largely maintained, and the paper honestly reports the accuracy-fairness trade-off.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: reducing PSCF to the conditional-independence constraint I(S;X|Y)=0 yields a training objective that is essentially standard conditional adversarial debiasing / fair-representation learning. The mechanism (adversarial generator/discriminator, per-pixel masking) is very close to the AD and FAAP baselines being compared against, so the distinction is largely interpretive rather than a new algorithm.

Theoretical soundness of Theorem 1 is questionable. The proof (Eq. 19) uses P(X|Y, do(Δs|π_d)) = P(X|Y, Δs), i.e., it treats a path-specific intervention as equivalent to conditioning on S, which is a known subtlety and is generally invalid. It also assumes X is a complete mediator (P(Ŷ|X,Y)=P(Ŷ|X)). The derivability claim is therefore not fully rigorous, and the paper only partially acknowledges this.

The SCM in Fig. 1 posits an edge Y → X (the label causes the input), which is unusual and unjustified for imaging data; the entire path-specific argument (indirect path S → Y → X → Ŷ) hinges on this non-standard structure that is not defended.

No empirical comparison to the PSCF method being extended (Chiappa et al. [9]) — even in the synthetic setting only Vanilla and AD are compared, so it is unclear how SPARC relates to the approach it claims to make scalable.

The paper itself states SPARC is stricter than PSCF (it removes all residual S-dependence in X given Y, not only the component propagating to Ŷ), so the 'path-specific' framing is somewhat overstated relative to what the objective actually enforces.

Reported fairness gains are consistent but modest, and could plausibly follow from the stricter conditional-invariance objective rather than genuine path-specific behavior; the interpretation that improvements are 'primarily due to the path-specific nature' is not directly isolated by an ablation.

Minor issues: the code URL on page 3 is blank; the theory targets the MI-form EOd but the paper also reports EOp and DP, which are not addressed by the theorems, creating a slight mismatch between claims and evidence.
